why: Distance-based and gradient-based models give wrong or slow results when one feature is measured in lakhs and another in single digits.
explain: Imagine comparing customers by income (₹2,00,000–₹50,00,000) and age (20–70). In a distance calculation, income differences are thousands of times larger, so age is effectively ignored.
**Standardisation** (z-score) rescales each feature to mean 0 and standard deviation 1. It is the default choice.
**Min-max normalisation** rescales to the range 0–1. It is useful when you need bounded inputs, but it is sensitive to outliers.

**Need scaling**: k-NN, k-means, SVM, PCA, regularised regression, neural networks, anything trained with gradient descent. **Do not need it**: decision trees, random forests and gradient boosting, because they split one feature at a time.

formula.plain: Subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation: "how many SDs from average".

example.title: Standardising a new customer with StandardScaler
steps: Age: mean 40, SD 8.165 (StandardScaler divides by n) → new customer aged 55: z = (55 − 40) / 8.165 ≈ 1.84
The customer becomes (1.84, −0.74): both numbers now in "standard deviation" units
example.result: Two features whose units differed by a factor of tens of thousands now sit on the same scale, so neither dominates a distance by accident. The chapter's next example shows the payoff: unscaled, k-NN thinks B (60 yrs, ₹6.5 lakh) is 12× closer to A (25 yrs, ₹6 lakh) than C (27 yrs, ₹12 lakh); scaled, C wins (1.52 vs 2.74).

mistakes: Fitting the scaler on all data, including the test set (leakage). Fit on training data only.
Scaling for tree models: harmless, but wasted effort.
takeaways: Distance and gradient methods need scaling
Fit the scaler on training data only, inside a pipeline

practice.code:
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
import numpy as np
X_train = np.array([[30, 400000], [40, 900000], [50, 1500000]])
sc = StandardScaler().fit(X_train)             # fit on training data only
print(sc.mean_.round().tolist(), sc.scale_.round(3).tolist())  # [40.0, 933333.0] [8.165, 449691.252]
print(sc.transform([[55, 600000]]).round(2))   # [[ 1.84 -0.74]]
